extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent attorneys/agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on anticipating patent claims under 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty) including when single or multiple references apply, genus-species and ranges issues, inherency, pre‑AIA 102(a) specifics, and ways to overcome such rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — every element in a single reference
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 when the invention is anticipated (not novel) over a disclosure available as prior art. To reject a claim as anticipated by a reference, the disclosure must teach every element required by the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference.” (Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil). The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the claim; elements must be arranged as required by the claim (but ipsissimis verbis identity of terminology is not required). See MPEP § 2131 and case law (e.g., Richardson v. Suzuki; In re Bond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not ipsissimis verbis test (terminology flexibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements must be arranged as required by the claim, but identity of terminology is not required; the test is not ipsissimis verbis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Bond and related cases: identity of terminology is not necessary so long as the reference discloses the elements and arrangement required by the claim. Examiners should analyze whether the reference sufficiently describes the claimed elements, not whether it uses the exact words of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-reference 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections — limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally only one reference should be used in making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102. However, a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection over multiple references is proper when extra references are cited to (A) prove primary reference contains an 'enabled disclosure,' (B) explain the meaning of a term used in the primary reference, or (C) show that a characteristic not disclosed in the reference is inherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2131.01. If multiple references are used, the role of each must be clear (enablement, term meaning, or inherency). Examiners should follow subsections I-III for how to apply extrinsic/other references or evidence in each circumstance; case law includes In re Samour, In re Donohue, Baxter Travenol, Continental Can, Atlas Powder, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extra references to prove the primary reference contains an 'enabled disclosure'
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional reference may be relied on to show that the primary reference has an 'enabled disclosure' when the claimed composition or machine is disclosed identically by the reference but methods or enabling details are missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: In re Samour; In re Donohue — publication teaching structure plus patents teaching methods of making the class. If the publication teaches all claim elements, motivation to combine is not required; patents may be submitted to show what was publicly known that would enable the primary reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extra references or extrinsic evidence to explain meaning of a term in the primary reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence may be used to explain (but not expand) the meaning of terms and phrases used in the primary reference relied upon as anticipatory prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Baxter Travenol — extrinsic evidence (depositions, declarations, admissions) showed what 'commercial blood bags' meant. Actelion v. Mylan: where claims/specification/prosecution history do not clarify a term's precision, courts may consult extrinsic evidence to understand the meaning of the term to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time. Do not use extrinsic evidence to broaden a reference beyond what it teaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extra references or evidence to show inherency
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra references or extrinsic evidence can be used to show that a characteristic not expressly disclosed in the primary reference is inherently present in what the reference describes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherency evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described in the reference and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill. Failure of contemporaneous recognition does not preclude inherency (Continental Can; Atlas Powder). Examine test data and expert testimony; see MPEP § 2112 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species: a species will anticipate a genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic (genus) claim cannot be allowed if the prior art discloses a species falling within the claimed genus — the species will anticipate the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: In re Slayter; In re Gosteli. If a prior art reference discloses a specific species within a claimed genus, the genus claim is anticipated unless entitlement to an earlier priority date exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species named in a reference anticipates the species claim regardless of how many species are listed
rubrics_metrics.description: When the species is clearly named in a reference, the species claim is anticipated no matter how many other species are additionally named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ex parte A — a compound specifically named among many compounds is still 'described' for anticipation purposes (Merck Index analogy). In re Sivaramakrishnan also supports this principle; unexpected properties of the species do not negate anticipation if the species was disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic disclosure anticipates a species only if the species can be 'at once envisaged'
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure will anticipate a claimed species covered by that disclosure when the species can be 'at once envisaged' from the disclosure — i.e., when a person of ordinary skill can immediately draw the structural formula or write the name of each compound included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kennametal; In re Petering; In re Schauman. Factors include how limited/well-delineated the classes of substituents are, the number of alternatives at each position, preferred embodiments and whether the disclosure contemplates the particular combination. If enumerating and combining teachings within a generic formula is necessary to arrive at the species, anticipation is appropriate only where the classes are sufficiently limited so the species is readily identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of ranges — specific example within claimed range anticipates
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers several compositions by recitation of ranges is anticipated if one specific example within the prior art falls within the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner: an actual prior art data point within a claimed compositional range anticipates the range. See also UCB, Inc. v. Actavis Labs. UT, Inc. If the prior art discloses a point within the claimed range, the prior art anticipates the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of ranges — overlapping/touching ranges require 'sufficient specificity'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prior art teaches a range overlapping or touching the claimed range but provides no specific examples within the claimed range, anticipation depends on whether the prior art range discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' (case-by-case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider the narrowness of the claimed range and other facts; cases include ClearValue (anticipated where no evidence of criticality across range) and Atofina (not anticipatory where claimed narrow range was shown critical). If unclear, an examiner may make both a §102 and §103 statement and must explain reasons for anticipation and an obviousness analysis. See MPEP § 2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very close but non-overlapping prior art ranges do not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art that teaches a value or range very close to, but not overlapping or touching, the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires exact disclosure of what is claimed; differences between the prior art disclosure and the claim mean the rejection must be based on §103 (obviousness) rather than §102. Titanium Metals example: non-overlapping data points led to obviousness, not anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations are irrelevant to 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations (e.g., unexpected results, commercial success) is irrelevant to 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections and thus cannot overcome a rejection based on anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Wiggins: secondary considerations may be relevant to nonobviousness under §103 but are immaterial for §102 anticipation analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonanalogous art or 'teaching away' does not prevent anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that alleged anticipatory prior art is nonanalogous, teaches away, or addressed a different problem are not germane to a §102 anticipation rejection; a reference can be anticipatory even if it disparages the invention or is from a different field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twin Disc; State Contracting & Eng'g; Celeritas; Upsher-Smith Labs; Atlas Powder: the focus is whether the reference explicitly or inherently discloses every limitation in the claims, regardless of its field or whether it later disparages the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) — 'known or used' means publicly known/used
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), 'known or used' means knowledge or use accessible to the public (i.e., not deliberately kept secret).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carella v. Starlight Archery; W. L. Gore & Assoc. — public accessibility is the key. See MPEP § 2128 et seq. for public accessibility case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) — sale of product made by secret process may be public use if process can be determined from product
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonsecret use of a claimed process in producing articles for commercial purposes is a public use; secret use coupled with sale does not result in public use unless the public could learn the claimed process by examining the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examination of the product would reveal the process, sale can create a public use; otherwise secret process + sale does not create a §102(a) bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) — 'in this country' means within the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: For pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejections, only knowledge or use in the United States can be relied upon; foreign knowledge/use cannot form the basis for a §102(a) rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Ekenstam and related guidance: 'in this country' is interpreted as the United States only (not other WTO/NAFTA members) for pre-AIA §102(a) purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) — 'by others' means any entity different from the inventive entity
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Others' in pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) refers to any authors/inventors different from the inventive entity; it is sufficient that the entity differs by one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation preserves the one-year grace period under §102(b). It applies to all types of prior art references under pre-AIA §102(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection — available remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a pre-AIA §102 rejection by: (A) persuasively arguing claims are patentably distinguishable; (B) amending claims to patentably distinguish; (C) filing a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration showing prior invention (when applicable); (D) filing a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit/declaration showing the reference invention was derived from the applicant; (E) submitting and perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); (F) submitting and perfecting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2131.01 and § 2132.01. Note restrictions: 1.131 is not appropriate against certain U.S. patents/publications claiming interfering subject matter; evidence and procedural requirements for affidavits/declarations are discussed in MPEP § 715 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing a reference's disclosure was derived from the inventor — requirements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a reference's disclosure was derived from the inventor (so it is not 'by others'), an applicant may submit affidavits/declarations (e.g., under 37 CFR 1.132) establishing that the reference's relevant subject matter originated from the inventor or a joint inventor, but mere naked assertions are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Katz and related cases: declarations should provide context, explanation, and supporting evidence; research-paper coauthor situations require careful analysis (students doing testing may not be inventors). If a co-author refuses to disclaim inventorship or presents contrary evidence, the applicant may fail to overcome the rejection. Options also include adding coauthors as joint inventors if statutory requirements are met. See EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen (naked assertions insufficient) and Ex parte Kroger (coauthor disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit — swearing back to overcome some pre-AIA 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference is not a statutory bar under pre-AIA §§102(b),(c),(d), an applicant can overcome a pre-AIA §102 rejection by swearing back of the reference via a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit showing prior invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of 1.131 is subject to applicability limitations (e.g., not appropriate when the reference is a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that should be treated under pre-AIA §102(e)). See MPEP § 715 for the requirements of 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits and MPEP § 2136.05 for related §102(e) issues.
